ordersBacklog.title: Net sales orders, homes closed & backlog
ordersBacklog.content:
Net sales orders are new home contracts signed in the period (before cancellations); homes closed are deliveries that convert to revenue; backlog is the stock of signed-but-undelivered homes, the forward order book.

For Lennar: orders are the leading indicator -- management flagged net sales orders down roughly 9% YoY in Q3 FY2026 as elevated mortgage rates and weak affordability kept buyers on the sidelines, well before it shows up in closings or revenue.

What to watch:

  • Orders falling faster than closings -- backlog starts shrinking and future revenue growth stalls
  • Backlog as a multiple of quarterly closings (coverage for the next 1-2 quarters)

asp.title: Average selling price
asp.content:
Average price per home across closings (revenue this period), new orders (what's being signed now) and backlog (what's still to be delivered).

For Lennar: ASP has been drifting down as the company leans into entry-level, affordable product and uses price cuts -- not just incentives -- to keep volume moving; new-orders ASP below backlog ASP signals further mix-driven price erosion ahead.

What to watch:

  • Orders ASP trending below backlog/closings ASP (price cuts still working through the pipeline)
  • ASP decline versus unit growth -- is revenue held up by volume or by price

marginIncentive.title: Home sales margin, incentives & cancellations
marginIncentive.content:
Home sales gross margin is revenue less direct cost of the homes delivered (before SG&A); sales incentives (rate buydowns, price concessions, closing-cost assistance) as a percent of revenue is the discount builders give to move volume; the cancellation rate is contracts signed but walked away from.

For Lennar: home sales gross margin has compressed from roughly 17.8% a year earlier to the mid-15% range as incentives running 12-14%+ of sales price are used to defend volume against ~7%+ mortgage rates -- the central margin story for FY2026.

What to watch:

  • Incentives rising while margin keeps falling -- discounting that isn't working
  • Cancellation rate spiking -- buyers can't close even after signing (qualification/rate risk)

segmentRevenue.title: Segment revenue & Homebuilding operating income
segmentRevenue.content:
Lennar reports Homebuilding (home sales, ~93% of revenue), Financial Services (mortgage, title, closing -- fee income off Lennar's own buyers), Multifamily and Lennar Other (fund/proptech investments, mark-to-market).

For Lennar: Homebuilding operating income is the business; Financial Services is a high-margin, counter-cyclically useful add-on (it earns on every closing Lennar itself generates), while Multifamily and Lennar Other run near break-even to negative and swing on mark-to-market (e.g. technology-investment losses in weak quarters) -- noise around the real signal.

What to watch:

  • Homebuilding operating income as % of its own segment revenue -- the true margin trend, since the log axis compresses the small segments' swings
  • Financial Services revenue tracking Homebuilding closings (capture rate), not drifting apart

balanceSheet.title: Balance sheet
balanceSheet.content:
Shareholders' equity is assets less liabilities; plotted against total liabilities to show leverage.

For Lennar Corporation: equity that grows only through revaluations or share issues is not the same as retained earnings.

What to watch:

  • Liabilities growing faster than equity
  • Goodwill share of equity after acquisitions

cashDebt.title: Cash and debt
cashDebt.content:
Cash & equivalents against total borrowings (leases excluded unless noted).

For Lennar Corporation: the DCF's net-debt bridge uses these balances at the latest balance-sheet date.

What to watch:

  • Net debt trend versus EBITDA
  • Refinancing dates and covenants in the filings

ebitda.title: EBITDA
ebitda.content:
EBITDA is earnings before interest, tax, depreciation and amortisation -- an operating-cash proxy that ignores capital intensity.

For Lennar Corporation: read it beside CapEx: a business that must reinvest most of its EBITDA is not as cash-generative as the margin suggests.

What to watch:

  • EBITDA margin trend
  • Gap between EBITDA and operating cash flow (working capital)

epsDps.title: EPS and dividends
epsDps.content:
EPS is net income per share; DPS is the cash dividend paid per share. Both are in major currency units.

For Lennar Corporation: the payout ratio (DPS / EPS) shows how much of earnings is returned versus reinvested.

What to watch:

  • EPS growth versus net income growth (dilution)
  • Dividends funded from earnings, not debt

fcf.title: Free cash flow
fcf.content:
Reported FCF is operating cash flow less capital expenditure. Owner FCF (from the DCF) further deducts stock-based compensation, interest income and lease principal -- the cash an owner could actually take out.

For Lennar Corporation: the gap between net income and owner FCF is the earnings-quality question the valuation is built on.

What to watch:

  • FCF persistently below net income
  • Working-capital swings inflating one year's FCF

margins.title: Margins
margins.content:
Gross margin is revenue less cost of revenue; operating margin deducts operating expenses; net margin is after interest and tax.

For Lennar Corporation: the spread between gross and operating margin is the cost of running the business; a widening spread with flat gross margin means opex is growing faster than sales.

What to watch:

  • Direction of operating margin over several years, not one
  • One-offs (impairments, disposals) that distort net margin

ocfCapex.title: Operating cash flow and CapEx
ocfCapex.content:
Operating cash flow is cash generated by operations; CapEx is cash invested in fixed and intangible assets.

For Lennar Corporation: CapEx here is shown as stored (sign convention varies by ticker); the DCF splits it into stay-in-business and growth where disclosed.

What to watch:

  • CapEx rising faster than revenue
  • OCF that diverges from EBITDA

profit.title: Profit lines
profit.content:
Gross profit is revenue less cost of revenue; operating income deducts operating expenses; net income is after interest, tax and one-offs.

For Lennar Corporation: the three lines together show where margin is made and lost between the top line and the bottom.

What to watch:

  • Operating income growing slower than gross profit (opex creep)
  • Net income far from operating income (interest, tax, one-offs)

revenue.title: Revenue
revenue.content:
Revenue is the top line: what customers paid for goods and services in the period, before any costs.

For Lennar Corporation: the growth rate matters more than the level; compare it with the DCF's base-case growth path below.

What to watch:

  • Acceleration or deceleration in YoY growth
  • Whether growth is organic or acquired
  • Interim rows show seasonality

sbc.title: Stock-based compensation and share count
sbc.content:
Stock-based comp is the expense of equity awards; shares outstanding shows the dilution it causes net of buybacks.

For Lennar Corporation: the DCF charges SBC as a cash cost and holds the share count flat, so this chart is the check on that assumption.

What to watch:

  • Share count rising while buybacks are advertised
  • SBC as a percentage of revenue
